civs.name: Plith

script.direction: Top to bottom, left to right
script.note: Three glyphs across a line, as on Plith arms.

religions.name: Pidmeddom
religions.desc: Pidmeddom is the faith of the Aibmen, founded on the death of Pidmedmed the tracker. He followed the visitors from beyond the sky for nine days, judged them to be the children of the demon Oulvoam, and took his own life when they surrounded him. His followers hold that the visitors are scouts of an invasion. They live in fortified forest communities, charge outsiders for passage, and teach that a death freely chosen denies the enemy its prize.

religions.name: Walmeth
religions.desc: Walmeth is a secretive faith that hides its bloody rites beneath layers of deception. It teaches its adherents to doubt every truth except the knife's, and to shun the zealot and the open-hearted alike. Divine wisdom is sought in careful suspicion and solitary thought. The Walmeers are found in every trade and admit to none of it.

civs.origin: The Plith live inside the old western jungle and treat it as a wall. Most of them are brave, grasping and suspicious by creed: they charge strangers for passage, test every servant and guest, and read a bent stem or a silent bird as others read a page. About seven hundred years ago the visitors from beyond the sky were seen in their forest, and that revelation broke their faith in two. The followers of Pidmedmed the tracker, who judged the visitors to be demons and chose his own death, left the older Walmeth and became Pidmeddom, a religion fixed on the observers and on the invasion it expects. Walmeth stayed what it was: secretive, cynical and private. Their holy places reward cunning and devotion, and their archers and trackers are raised for one purpose, to see first.

observer.label: Hostile
observer.text: Both Plith religions hold that the visitors from beyond the sky are demons scouting an invasion. Paranoia is a virtue and trust a sin.

unit.name: Mmaiploun
unit.flavor: Forest archers named in the old tongue. They shoot from cover, move before the answer comes, and know every path an enemy might take to flee.

tech_a.name: Sign Lore
tech_a.desc: The Plith read the forest as others read a page. A bent stem, a silent bird, a mark cut low on a trunk: each is a sign, and children learn the signs before they learn their letters.

tech_b.name: The Nine-Day Canon
tech_b.desc: Nine days of questions, set down in the angular script and never altered. The Canon tells a ruler how to test a servant, a guest and a rumour, and in what order.

followers_desc: The Vigilant are honoured among the Plith. They are watchers of the forest paths, trained to read signs and to distrust a quiet day. Sharp in intrigue and learning and poor at courtesy, they suit a spymaster's seat or the chaplaincy.

The Mmaiploun Trackers are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from Ngeelkuin. Masters of Sign Lore, wary and brave at once, they follow a trail through forest or jungle for days. They make the best spymasters the Plith can raise, and hold a wooded line in war.
civs.tagline: Watchful forest people of Ngeelkuin, sworn against the visitors from the sky.

civs.name: Queekwa

script.medium: Leaves, wood carvings and opaque ink on fabric
script.direction: Top to bottom, columns right to left
script.note: Glyphs stack in columns read top to bottom: a medium or large sign over smaller ones. Columns follow one another from right to left.

religions.name: Kaliska
religions.desc: Kaliska is a faith of armed judges who walk the ancient pilgrim roads of the old forest, carrying both a healer's skill and a sword. Its adherents follow a strict code of justice in the name of the god Mawku and hold that courage means defending those who cannot defend themselves. A Kalisim court may convene at any roadside shrine. Its verdicts are spoken aloud, written in the Cej, and enforced on the spot.

civs.origin: The Queekwa are the people of the ancient pilgrim roads of the forest. They farm the clearings, keep the shrines and the houses along the way and trade with whoever walks past, and what they share is a sense of duty: justice, courage and compassion are to them one obligation, and they measure themselves by how well they defend those who cannot defend themselves. The figure they honour most is the armed judge who walks from shrine to shrine with a healer's kit and a sword, hears a case where it happened and enforces the ruling on the spot. Their lords are sworn households of knights more than states, and their holy places make better knights and better diplomats. To outsiders they are fair and predictable, which is rarer on Thekan than strength.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Kaliska takes no position on the visitors. A road judge rules on deeds, whoever commits them.

unit.name: Wardens
unit.flavor: Armed keepers of the roads. They are patrolmen before they are soldiers, hard to surprise and slow to break, though no one would call them a battle line.

tech_a.name: Wound-Binding
tech_a.desc: A judge who rides the roads must also keep the wounded alive until the hearing. The Queekwa bind, stitch and splint with a skill that began as a duty of the court.

tech_b.name: The Road Codex
tech_b.desc: Every ruling given on the road is written into one book, so that the same wrong meets the same answer in every village. The faithful hold the Codex to be an act of worship.

followers_desc: The Road Judges are honoured among the Queekwa. They walk the roads between settlements, settle quarrels where they find them and bear arms to see the verdict kept. Fair speakers and able captains with little taste for secrets, they serve well as marshal, court physician or knight.

The Circuit Arbiters are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from Ngeelkuin. Each has walked the whole circuit for years, judging by day and binding wounds by night. Just and brave, they come as healers or forest fighters and can lead a host or keep a court in health.
civs.tagline: A forest people of the old pilgrim roads, who hold justice, courage and care for the weak to be one duty.

civs.name: Pfaunkti

script.note: Small carved letters run in short rows.

religions.name: Deaulnueilkih
religions.desc: Deaulnueilkih is a faith of builders and mothers. Its adherents honour the god Deaulnueilk through patient creation, from the birthing chamber to the slowly rising temple, and hold that pleasure, carefully cultivated, is as sacred as labour. Every stone is expected to show the hand that set it. The Deaulnueilkirm believe the gods favour those who join delight to diligence, and distrust anything done in haste.

religions.name: Sinchidi
religions.desc: Sinchidi is a faith of solitary tower-dwellers. In tall stone keeps marked with ancient star-signs, the Sinchis keep vigil beside the whispers of their dead and record what the heavens decree. They cultivate perfect stillness of heart beneath the distant light of the god Zuaivue. Each tower holds one scholar, one lamp and a record that began before the scholar was born.

civs.origin: The Pfaunkti see the world as unfinished work. Whatever their trade, farmer, mason, potter or clerk, they generally prize calm, stubbornness and diligence, distrust anything done in haste, and expect a thing to show the hand that made it. Building is the craft they honour most, and a well set stone is their idea of a good name. Pleasure, carefully cultivated, is as sacred to them as labour. Their other face is solitary: scholars who live one to a tower beside a single lamp, keeping records that began before they were born and writing down what the heavens decree. Their holy places make the land prosper and reward learning. They do not preach to the sky or fear it. They set their walls by its turning and raise towers to hear it.

observer.label: Listening
observer.text: No doctrine names the visitors, but the Sinchis record what the heavens decree, and Pfaunkti towers are raised to hear the sky.

unit.name: Spears
unit.flavor: Masons who carry spears to the wall they built. They give little ground and expect none, and they fight best where there is stone at their backs.

tech_a.name: Star-Aligned Masonry
tech_a.desc: The Pfaunkti set their stones to the turning of the sky. A wall laid on the right night stands without mortar, and the builders waste neither stone nor labour finding out why.

tech_b.name: The Listening Towers
tech_b.desc: Towers raised to hear rather than to see. From their tops the Pfaunkti claim to catch what the sky is saying, and a ruler who owns such a tower is listened to in turn.

followers_desc: The Stone-Setters are honoured among the Pfaunkti. They cut and set the stones of the high places and keep the count of every course laid. Diligent, calm and unwarlike, they are stewards first and last.

The Master Builders are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from Ngeelkuin. They align walls to the stars and raise what lesser hands only repair. Diligent and calm, each is an architect or a military engineer, and none is better placed than as steward of a realm that builds.
civs.tagline: A patient, stubborn people who trust slow work, set their stones by the stars and raise towers to listen.

civs.name: Gleuncti

script.medium: Varied: an advanced people who write on many materials
script.direction: Left to right, top to bottom
script.note: Consonants stand on the line. Vowels hang above and between them.

religions.name: Ineoism
religions.desc: Ineoism is the faith of the temple-citadels, where priest-kings rule as living vessels of the law of Igu. Its scholars read the sacred Meen literally, and its communities value restraint, shared celebration and the keeping of traditional bounds. A ruler's piety is believed to shine outward as radiance that draws tribute from lesser lords. From the fertile lands to the desert, the authority of an Ineoist king is measured by how far his light is said to reach.

religions.name: Auncuance
religions.desc: Auncuance was founded on the testimony of a scholar renowned for never lying. He saw celestial knights descend in silver armour, test the water and the air, then remove their shining shells to swim as mortals. From this his followers learned that truth lives unclothed, and that walls and garments stand between a person and real existence. The Auncuors live close to nature, wear crowns of silver foil in memory of the knights, and expect them to return as friends.

civs.origin: The Gleuncti are the people of the temple-citadels and the most numerous civilization of western Thekan. Most of them work the fields and markets that feed the citadels, and they generally value contentment, shared celebration and the keeping of old bounds. At their centre stand priest-kings whose piety is said to shine outward as a radiance that draws tribute from lesser lords, and their holy places reward learning and renown. Beside them lives a younger faith, founded on a truthful scholar who saw celestial knights in silver armour descend, test the water and swim as mortals. Its followers live close to nature, wear crowns of silver foil and expect the knights to return as friends. Between the citadel and the unwalled camp, the Gleuncti hold the most hopeful view of the sky on Thekan.

observer.label: Welcoming
observer.text: Auncuance was founded on a sighting of celestial knights and holds that the Watchers are saviours who will return as friends. Ineoism has not ruled on the matter.

unit.name: Guard
unit.flavor: The guard of the temple citadels. Heavily armoured and seldom seen beyond the walls, they exist so that a holy place never has to ask for help.

tech_a.name: Silver-Shell Lore
tech_a.desc: The shining shells of the old shore are ground, read and kept in the temples. The Gleuncti hold that the pattern inside a shell is the first scripture.

tech_b.name: Sky-Metal Forging
tech_b.desc: Iron that fell from the sky is rare, and the Gleuncti forge it only for those who have earned it. A blade of sky-metal is given, never sold.

followers_desc: The Temple Witnesses are honoured among the Gleuncti. They stand at rites and oaths and speak only of what they saw. Honest or patient by habit and hopeless at plotting, they fit the chaplain's office or the chancellor's.

The Radiant Voices are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Greenbelt. They carry the teaching of the temples to other courts, and their word is taken as given. Honest and patient, a Voice is a theologian or a diplomat and belongs beside the ruler as chaplain or chancellor.
civs.tagline: The numerous people of the temple-citadels, fond of feasts and old bounds, and hopeful about the sky.

civs.name: Ioddrik

script.note: A pure abjad. The reading of vowels is standardized, so vowels are left out completely. Words are roots of three or four consonants, written right to left with spaces between them.

religions.name: Pietlieism
religions.desc: Pietlieism is a warrior faith of the desert riders, devoted to the god Teovei and to the bond between those who fight together. Its adherents gather in great halls called jitlies to share sacred wine and recount their battles, and hold that courage is a gift of fellowship, never of the lone hero. The golden sword is its sign. A Pietliei who faces a trial alone is thought to have failed it already.

religions.name: Rabi
religions.desc: Rabi is the faith of the open desert. Five sun-blessed temple-courts stand in the desert as seats of justice, and from them wandering judges ride out at the desert's own pace, carrying ancient law and a tempered blade. They are known for meeting hardship with serene hearts and for showing mercy while they guard the sacred wastes against trespass. A traveller in the deep desert is under Rabi law whether he knows it or not.

civs.origin: The Ioddrik are the people of the deep desert. They know how to dig for water, and how to find and use the caves that lie across the Choraman. They hold that courage is a gift of fellowship, never of the lone hero: fighters gather in great halls to share sacred wine and recount their battles, and a trial faced alone is counted as already failed. Law rides with them too. Wandering judges cross the wastes at the desert's own pace, carrying ancient law and a tempered blade, serene in hardship and merciful in judgment. Their leaders gather warriors by faith and fame, not gold, and their holy places sharpen commanders. To the Ioddrik the desert is sacred ground, and every traveller on it is under their law.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Neither desert faith has a teaching on the visitors. Trespass on the sacred wastes is judged the same for all.

unit.name: Ratta
unit.flavor: Riders of the deep desert on lean Corri bred for sand and thirst. They are fast, patient, and at home where an enemy is already dying.

tech_a.name: Deep Wells
tech_a.desc: Wells sunk deeper than anyone else will dig, and covered so that the desert does not take them back. An Ioddrik host drinks where others find dust.

tech_b.name: The Well Chain
tech_b.desc: Wells joined underground by a sloping tunnel, so that water runs from the hills to the plain without seeing the sun. Along each tunnel stands a line of watered halts a day apart, and men called to arms follow it and arrive fit to fight.

followers_desc: The Vruagmar are honoured among the Ioddrik. They are desert captains who study the wells before they study the enemy. Just or calm, learned soldiers with no patience for intrigue, they serve as marshal or commander.

The Ratta Aya are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Choraman. They hold the knowledge of the deep wells and decide where a host can live. Just and calm, a desert warrior or an expert of open ground, a Ratta Aya is the marshal a dry realm needs.
civs.tagline: A deep-desert people who know where the water is, bound by fellowship and old law.

civs.name: Qormaic

script.direction: Left to right or top to bottom
script.note: Letters as drawn for the coat of arms, in two rows. The Qormaic have no heraldic signs of their own and use the common heraldry of the Choraman, sparingly.

religions.name: Uheaia
religions.desc: Uheaia is a faith of warrior-priestesses among the western desert riders. Its adherents seek harmony with the wild through visitation by spirits, which the goddess Kiogreaom sends to those strong and pure enough to bear them. Sanctuaries stand in untamed places, and their keepers are tall, formidable women who cast out corruption by force of arms. Among the Uheaii, holiness is something a person must be able to carry.

civs.origin: The Qormaic are a people of the western desert, a confederation of clans that has grown into something close to an aristocracy. They are led by warrior-priestesses, tall and formidable women who keep sanctuaries in untamed places and cast out corruption by force of arms. Holiness, to them, is something a person must be strong and pure enough to carry, and they choose their lines accordingly. As a rule they are bold, content with their place and at ease in the wild. Leaders draw the finest warriors through personal trust and shared renown, and their holy places reward a ruler for the knights who stand with her.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Uheaia speaks of spirits sent by the goddess, not of visitors from the sky.

unit.name: Priestess Riders
unit.flavor: Priestesses who ride to war on desert-bred Corri. They are heavy for riders and incredibly fierce, made to break an enemy in close fighting more than to run him down.

tech_a.name: Spirit-Smoke
tech_a.desc: Resins and herbs burned in the sanctuaries until the air itself is holy. The Qormaic say the spirits come to the smoke, and that the faithful can feel them arrive.

tech_b.name: The Deep Vision
tech_b.desc: The long trance of the priestesses, entered through the smoke and returned from with answers. One who has seen so far is not easily troubled by the day.

followers_desc: The Keepers are honoured among the Qormaic. They guard the spirit places of the Choraman and learn the rites along with the blade. Brave or content with little, strong in arms and lore and careless of property, they serve as knights or court chaplains.

The Exorcist-Priestesses are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Choraman. They drive out spirits with smoke and steel and fear neither. Brave and content, a desert warrior or a mystic, each can stand as champion or lead the rites of the court.
civs.tagline: A proud people of the western desert, who follow warrior-priestesses.

civs.name: Xacra

script.note: A pure abjad cut in stone. Only consonants are written, from right to left and without spaces. A small cut mark divides one word from the next.

religions.name: Cajii
religions.desc: Cajii is the faith of the Otija peoples, who revere the Otij, the great scaled predators of their homeland, which they ride to war and hunt on foot. The god Otij Ondeong is held to grant rebirth in scale and claw to those who die facing them. Two orders lead to that grace: the Feqits, the Brotherhood of Spears, and the Qijits, the Sisterhood of Beasts. Every scar is counted as progress toward the next life.

religions.name: Ocacxi
religions.desc: Ocacxi is the faith of the Appa and their kin in the green-stone mountains, pale descendants of an ancient people who survived by hiding. They worship Urvu among megaliths that guard the old paths, and believe their bloodline carries a birthright bought with centuries of endurance. The stones are said to remember every betrayal. In the halls of the Mountain Empire, patience and vengeance are counted as one virtue.

civs.origin: The Xacra are two peoples under one script. In the green-stone mountains live the pale descendants of an ancient people who survived by hiding. They keep megaliths that are said to remember every betrayal, count patience and vengeance as one virtue, rule cavern cities beneath the peaks and ride the great shelled beetles of their valleys. South of them live the Otija, a people once less advanced in their crafts, who were inspired by their neighbours, took up some of their ways and came to form a single civilization with them. They turned the taming arts of the ancients on the Otij, the scaled predators of the southern Malachites and the lands below, and have since made those methods their own. They ride the Otij to war, hunt them on foot and hope to be reborn in scale and claw. Every scar is progress toward the next life. The two keep a bond of mutual gain, and neither forgives easily.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Neither the megalith faith nor the beast faith has a teaching on the visitors.

unit.name: Scale-Beast Riders or Shell-Beast Riders
unit.flavor: The Xacra ride the beasts of the Malachite Mountains: scaled runners for one religion, shelled giants for the other.

tech_a.name: Beast-Breaking
tech_a.desc: The great beasts of the mountains do not serve, neither the scaled runners of one religion nor the shelled giants of the other. The Xacra have learned to break one to the saddle without breaking its temper, and the rider who survives the lesson is worth ten.

tech_b.name: War-Herd Driving
tech_b.desc: A single beast is a terror. A herd driven the same way is an army that feeds itself, and the Xacra have learned to turn one without being trampled.

followers_desc: The Beast-Grooms are honoured among the Xacra. They raise the great beasts of the Malachite Mountains from the egg and carry the scars to prove it. Brave or quick to anger, hard fighters and poor talkers, they serve as knights and commanders.

The Beast-Masters are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Malachite Mountains. They break beasts that kill their grooms and ride them where no road goes. Brave and wrathful, a Beast-Master is a hunter or an expert of rough ground, best placed as champion or as leader of a mountain host.
civs.tagline: Mountain keepers of old grudges and the beast riders who share their land.

civs.name: Aiexqelt

script.direction: Top to bottom in square blocks, columns and blocks right to left
script.note: An abjad set in square blocks of four consonants: two down the right column, then two down the left. Blocks follow one another from right to left, with clear space between them. A column may close on a decorative ending form that stands for no sound. Consonants are stamped or inked in a contrasting colour. Vowels are added in coloured ink, in the shape each faction has chosen. Dots and circles are the old, classical way.

religions.name: Dath
religions.desc: Dath is the ancient faith of the Eniol empire, a religion of law in which justice exists to serve order. The Dathiol honour technological progress and strict hierarchy together and accept deception and measured severity as tools of civilised rule. Four paths compete to define it: the tradition of Enfu, the central authority of Dexa, the learned elite of Cic and the reform of Pus. Each claims to be the empire's future.

civs.origin: The Aiexqelt are the Eniol, a people who once ruled half of Thekan and took tribute from the rest. Their empire declined slowly and then broke into four realms, each certain that it alone can restore the whole. Their faith is a religion of law in which justice exists to serve order, and it accepts deception and measured severity as tools of civilised rule. As a rule they are precise, calculating and proud of procedure: the letter of the law, the useful loophole and the memory of empire shape everything they do. Their lands are the most developed on the continent, and their holy places reward intrigue and control. They look at everyone else as former subjects.

observer.label: Divided
observer.text: Panth teaches that its god was born of a being from beyond the sky and welcomes the visitors as returning kin. The other three paths of Dath do not.

unit.name: Regiment
unit.flavor: A regiment raised and paid by one faction of the empire. Drilled, uniform and loyal to its paymasters, it fights in close order and dislikes rough ground.

tech_a.name: Scaled Plans
tech_a.desc: A building is first drawn small, to a fixed scale, with every stone counted and every beam measured before one is cut. The builder orders what the plan asks for and nothing more, and work once done by eye is no longer done twice.

tech_b.name: The Eniol Method
tech_b.desc: Eniol builders work from tested rules: how thick a wall must be for its height, how wide an arch may span, how much water a channel carries. Mills, lifts and drained fields built by these rules keep working, and land that works every season pays every season.

followers_desc: The Clerks of the Law are honoured among the Aiexqelt. They keep the rolls of Eniol and know which clause binds whom. Good with accounts and with quiet leverage, no use in a fight, they serve as steward or spymaster.

The Jurists are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from Eniol. They read the law of the fallen empire in full and can turn it to either side. Just in form and deceitful in practice, a Jurist is an administrator or a schemer, fit to run a treasury or a web of informers.
civs.tagline: Heirs of a fallen empire of law, split four ways over how to restore it.

civs.name: Veuqrit

script.medium: Brush and stamp on leaf paper and fabric
script.direction: Top to bottom, one word to a line, each word right to left
script.note: Each sign is one unbroken brush stroke. The brush always lands at the upper right and leaves at the lower left. The first move after landing gives the consonant and the move that follows gives the vowel. Prefixes and suffixes widen a meaning greatly or mark grammar such as case. A line holds one short word read from right to left, and each new word starts a new line below.

religions.name: Vuvata
religions.desc: Vuvata is a faith of scholars and jurists, known for the largest collections of legal and theological writing on Thekan. Its adherents spend years in solitary study in the elbeivs, producing careful commentaries on the Vuv, and prefer the written word to the spoken in almost all dealings. The Meritocratic Forum draws its examiners from Vuvata monasteries. Rank among the Weji is earned at a desk.

civs.origin: The Veuqrit are the smallest of the twenty-one and among the most read. They are growers, craftsmen, paper makers and guards as much as any people, but learning is what they honour: their scholars and jurists have produced the largest body of legal and theological writing on Thekan, and in almost all dealings they prefer the written word to the spoken. Most are shy, patient and calm by creed, and many spend years in solitary study. They invented a paper made of plant leaves, glued, fermented and then brightened or darkened, and they write on it with brush and stamp. They are governed as a commonwealth of the proven, in which rank and reward follow the measured worth of a person to the whole, and the surest place to prove it is still a desk. They study everything that reaches them, the visitors from the sky included, and are slow to call anything an enemy before it has been properly described.

observer.label: Curious
observer.text: The Weji study everything, the visitors included. The Venata branch of Vuvata openly holds them to be benevolent.

unit.name: Archers
unit.flavor: Archers kept by the scholarly orders to guard their houses and presses. They are well trained and steady, and they are not meant to win a war alone.

tech_a.name: Pressed Glyphs
tech_a.desc: Glyphs cut in blocks and pressed into clay and paper, a hundred copies where a scribe made one. The Veuqrit were first to do it, and they are known for it.

tech_b.name: The Dilemma of Visitor Studies
tech_b.desc: The orders keep a few objects that no smith or glassmaker of this world could have made, and they have argued for generations whether to study them or seal them away. Those who study them have learned to weigh, measure and copy what they can: a metal that does not rust, a lens ground truer than any before. Who made them, and why, the orders have not yet agreed.

followers_desc: The Sages are honoured among the Veuqrit. They copy and keep the pressed tablets and would rather read than be heard. Patient or shy, learned and orderly and useless in war, they serve as court chaplain or steward.

The Scholars are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Southern Plains. They have read the whole archive of pressed glyphs and can find the one tablet that settles a matter. Patient and shy, shrewd or an administrator, a Scholar guides the faith of the court or its accounts.
civs.tagline: A small, bookish people, among whom rank follows proven worth.

civs.name: Aelwrid

script.medium: Punched metal foil, hot-iron brands on leather and wood, paint on cloth
script.note: The star-rod script: each consonant is a rod tipped with stars, and each vowel a small sun at its shoulder. A vowel before the rod sits on its left, and two vowels may merge into one sun, as the ring and dot of "ae" do here. The stars are struck with a punch and the rods scored between them, or the whole sign is burned in with a heated iron. This line reads "Aelwrid".

religions.name: Votie
religions.desc: Votie is a faith of the sun god Aedwoh, served by orders of healer-knights of the red desert. Its temples, the graorls, stand under sun-seals as places of healing and plain speech, and its adherents hold honesty and fierce compassion to be the same virtue seen from two sides. The Knight Circles of the region draw their oaths from it. A Votie blessing is not given to a liar.

religions.name: Merism
religions.desc: Merism orders its communities by birth-marks, which its priests read at birth to assign each person a role for life. Its adherents accept their place calmly and are known for mutual trust, little crime and steady soldiers. Most striking is its death rite: a Merist chooses the moment of his own end and meets it without fear. The knightly circles that share the faith consider this the root of their courage.

civs.origin: The Aelwrid are the sun-sworn of the red and gold desert north-east of the inner sea. They are a desert people of many trades, and what they generally share is plain honesty, a fierce kind of compassion and little fear of death. They serve a sun god whose orders of healer-knights hold honesty and compassion to be one virtue, and whose blessing is never given to a liar. Beside them stands a faith that reads a person's role from birth-marks and teaches each follower to choose the hour of their own death without fear. From both come sworn circles of knights, steady, trusting and hard to frighten, who go on foot in light mail made for the heat, quick over broken ground and at home in desert mountains. Their holy places make better knights and win the goodwill of strangers.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: The sun faiths have no teaching on the visitors.

unit.name: Sunsworn
unit.flavor: Knights of the healing circles, who fight on foot in light mail made for the desert. They cross broken ground quickly, outlast heavier troops in the heat, and they do not leave their wounded.

tech_a.name: Sun-Cautery
tech_a.desc: A wound closed with glass and sunlight does not rot. The knights of the Aelwrid carry the lens beside the sword and use both in the same hour.

tech_b.name: Knightly Physic
tech_b.desc: Before an Aelwrid squire is given a sword he learns the body: where the great vessels run, how a bone sets, how to stop bleeding and clean a wound. Every knight can treat himself and the man beside him, so fewer leave the field, and those who stay know exactly where to strike.

followers_desc: The Squires are honoured among the Aelwrid. They train under the sun in arms and in the care of the wounded, and are sworn to both. Compassionate or honest, strong fighters with no gift for deceit, they serve as knights or court physicians.

The Aedlwen are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Auric Barrens. They are the finished form of the Squire, who close wounds with the sun's fire and fight beside those they heal. Compassionate and honest, gallant or a physician, an Aedlwen is a champion on the field and a healer after it.
civs.tagline: Sun-sworn people of the red desert, honest, compassionate and unafraid of death.

civs.name: Qieulbaia

script.medium: Merchant marine marks on parchment and sails

religions.name: Qieulbai Nab
religions.desc: Qieulbai Nab is a faith of the stars. Its adherents, the Qieulbew, study the heavens with devotion under the goddess Pluielptia and believe wisdom comes to those who wait with open hearts. Every celestial sign is marked, since the stars are held to guide each person toward the best moments of a life. Patience and pleasure are regarded as the same skill, practised at different hours.

religions.name: Globism
religions.desc: Globism gives divine sanction to rule without restraint. It teaches that true power shows itself in unpredictable force, never in measured justice, and so legitimises both sudden violence and government by whim. The god Globi is held to favour those no one can anticipate. Among the clans a Globist chief is obeyed quickly, since no one knows what delay will cost.

religions.name: Qadi
religions.desc: Qadi is the faith of the Seru, sea raiders who own nothing and share everything they take, as the sea-gods require. Its adherents hold that glory belongs to those who laugh in battle and that the only lasting wealth is the fellowship of a brave crew. Plunder is divided at the mast. The Vieunn fleets that follow Ainkbu regard a rich man as someone who has not yet been visited.

civs.origin: The Qieulbaia are the people of the southern coasts. Most live in family clans bound by kinship and trade: fishers, shipwrights, growers and the merchant houses whose signs on sails became their written marks. They study the heavens with devotion, mark every celestial sign and believe wisdom comes to those who wait with open hearts. Not all of them wait. Some follow chiefs whose power lies in being impossible to predict, and some are sea raiders who own nothing, share everything they take and divide plunder at the mast. Patience, pleasure and sudden force all have a faith of their own here.

observer.label: Curious
observer.text: Old Qieulbaia poems hint that children of the visitors live among them. Aetmi, a branch of Qieulbai Nab, teaches it outright: some of the visitors came down and had children with the Qieulbaia, and their descendants are still among the people, believers or not.

unit.name: Raiders
unit.flavor: Raiders who come from the sea in fast crews. They hit a shore, take what can be carried and are back aboard before a levy can gather.

tech_a.name: Star Pilotage
tech_a.desc: Pilots who steer by the stars and name each one. The Qieulbaia sail at night, out of sight of land, and reach the harbour they intended.

tech_b.name: Open-Sea Reckoning
tech_b.desc: A knotted line cast astern to measure speed, a sand glass to measure time, and a pilot who keeps the sum of both. With it a fleet crosses open water in a straight line, by day or night, instead of following the coast.

followers_desc: The Crew-Brothers are honoured among the Qieulbaia. They row, raid and share the take as one crew. Brave or generous, fighters before anything else and bad with a ledger, they serve as knights and commanders.

The Navigators are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Southern Plains. They steer by the stars and bring a crew to the right beach on the right night. Brave and generous, a reaver or a forder, a Navigator leads raids and river crossings or fights at the prow.
civs.tagline: Star-reading family clans of the southern coasts, patient traders with raiders among them.

civs.name: Floicht

script.medium: Brush on bark and cloth, and carving in soft wood
script.direction: Top to bottom, left to right
script.note: Rounded letter forms made with a loaded brush, or cut with the same sweep into soft wood. Below them, heraldic signs.

religions.name: Oinmikounism
religions.desc: Oinmikounism keeps austere temples with no images in them, only the memory of wrongs and the promise of new beginnings. Its adherents practise disciplined patience, waiting for the proper moment either to protect new life or to end a life that has earned its fate. The god Cuaqkuin is held to keep both accounts. Oinmiounists are gentle with infants, exact with enemies and slow about both.

religions.name: Aitaga
religions.desc: Aitaga raises courage in battle above every other virtue and binds it to strong fellowship and reverence for ancestors. Its war-bands are known for fearless charges and for holding together when others break. The god Aita is honoured by deeds, and the dead are counted as members of the company. The Nijis hire out as soldiers across half of Thekan and are seldom the first to leave a field.

religions.name: Zdifft
religions.desc: Zdifft joins rigid law to dark mysticism under the stern god Outzdifft. Its clergy, the Log, serve as both judges and spiritual guides. They practise systematic doubt and use carefully measured suffering to bring out what they regard as deeper truths. Centuries of outside pressure have not altered their interpretations. In the spiritual centres of the Great Irchmo, law and pain are two instruments of the same enlightenment.

civs.origin: The Floicht are held together by one spiritual centre, which rules a wide federation through religious authority and tribute. They are a mixed people of growers, craftsmen, clerks and soldiers, and what they share is temperament: they are generally stubborn, hard to hurry and difficult to deceive. Their three faiths pull in different directions. The sternest joins rigid law to dark mysticism and uses measured suffering to bring out truth. Another keeps bare temples and a long patience, gentle with infants and exact with enemies. A third raises courage and fellowship above everything and hires its war-bands out across half of Thekan. They deal easily with other peoples. Many of them are highly literate, and with the Queekwa, the Veuqrit and the Aelwrid they stand among the foremost peoples of medicine on Thekan, known for their remedies and for their poisons.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: None of the three Floicht religions has ruled on the visitors.

unit.name: Niji Company
unit.flavor: A sworn company under strict discipline, every man entered in its log. They hold a line by rule, and the rule does not allow retreat.

tech_a.name: The Measure of Pain
tech_a.desc: The Floicht set down how much a body can bear, and at what point it begins to tell the truth. The record is exact, and it is consulted.

tech_b.name: The Tested Sickness
tech_b.desc: A sickness given on purpose to the willing, in a small measure, and written into the log. Companies treated so lose fewer men when the true sickness comes.

followers_desc: The Nijaik are honoured among the Floicht. They are company officers of the Auric Barrens, schooled as much as drilled, who hold to an order once it is given. Stubborn or just, able in war and letters and careless with coin, they serve as marshal or commander.

The Assayers are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Auric Barrens. They are the ones who tested the sickness: quiet mixers of remedies and poisons who know the measure of pain. Stubborn and just, every one a physician and each a schemer or a herbalist, they serve as spymaster or court physician.
civs.tagline: A stubborn, literate people gathered around one spiritual centre, known for remedies and for poisons.

civs.name: Qeomoq

script.direction: Left to right, one word to a line
script.note: Each sign is a small picture that stands for a syllable, with no letter parts inside it. A line holds one word read from left to right, and each new word starts a new line.

religions.name: Deteoure
religions.desc: Deteoure is a faith of mountain communes. Its adherents share all possessions and guard their privacy fiercely, and their settlements run on relentless work and unchanging routine. Each member labours for the wealth of all and withdraws afterward into silence and solitude. The Meritocratic Forum recruits from Deteoant communes, where advancement has always depended on what a person contributes.

civs.origin: The Qeomoq are commune people of the mountain waves north of the red desert. They share all possessions and guard their privacy fiercely. Land, tools and harvest belong to the settlement. Work is shared out in common and done with pride, on relentless effort and unchanging routine, and each member labours for the wealth of all and then withdraws into silence. Most are shy, diligent and stubborn by creed. The Meritocratic Forum that governs them recruits from the communes, where advancement has always depended on what a person contributes. They ask little of the outside world and expect it to ask little of them.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: The communes have no teaching on the visitors.

unit.name: Tapuqim
unit.flavor: The militia of the mountain communes, armed with long pikes. They are neighbours standing shoulder to shoulder, slow to strike and almost impossible to move.

tech_a.name: The Common Store
tech_a.desc: One granary for the whole commune, filled by all and opened by agreement. When the Qeomoq are called to arms, no one stays behind to guard his own bread.

tech_b.name: The Closed Mountain
tech_b.desc: Passes walled, paths hidden, terraces cut where no outsider would think to look. The Qeomoq build on their mountain with stone that is already there.

followers_desc: The Wardens are honoured among the Qeomoq. They look after the shared stores and the walls of the Wavecrest and prefer work to talk. Diligent or shy, steady with supplies and in defence, they serve as steward or commander.

The Stewards are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Wavecrest. They keep the common store, so that no hall eats while another starves. Diligent and shy, an overseer or an unyielding defender, a Steward runs the realm's holdings or holds its walls.
civs.tagline: Diligent, private commune people of the Wavecrest.

civs.name: Aigl

script.note: A plain alphabet of rounded letters, one for each sound, consonants and vowels alike, written in a line from left to right.

religions.name: Qavi
religions.desc: Qavi was born of hard conditions on a storm-beaten coast. It teaches survival through primal need and distrust, and its priests celebrate the flesh and ruthless instinct while training the faithful to question every truth and every claim of divinity, including their own. The god Eggav promises nothing to the weak. Qavists are scavengers, raiders and sceptics, and consider these three names for one sensible habit.

civs.origin: The Aigl are the Stormlanders, people of a rocky, storm-beaten coast. They fish, herd, salvage and build against the weather, and hard conditions made their faith: it teaches survival through need and distrust, celebrates the flesh and ruthless instinct, and trains the faithful to question every claim of divinity, including their own. Raiding is one more way through a bad year, and scavenger, raider and sceptic are to them three names for one sensible habit. On the coast their fighters raid from fast ships with a small core of knights. Those who turned inland follow warlords who measure a ruler by successful raids. They call witches to their courts and promise nothing to the weak. Some of them hold the visitors from the sky to be one more threat.

observer.label: Wary
observer.text: Qavi distrusts every claim of divinity. Two of its faiths, Wumi and Vuni, go further and hold the visitors to be a threat.

unit.name: Storm Raiders
unit.flavor: Raiders of the storm coast and the hills behind it, who move in weather no one else would march or sail in. They are quick, lightly armed and gone before the sky clears.

tech_a.name: Stormcraft
tech_a.desc: The Aigl do not pray for the storm to pass. They read it, store against it and march through it, and an Aigl army is still fed when others have turned back.

tech_b.name: The Sealed Coast
tech_b.desc: Sea walls, raised stores and drained ground, built by people who expect the flood every year. What the Aigl build is built to stand in water, and they build it cheaply.

followers_desc: The Witches are honoured among the Aigl. They read weather, brew remedies and know what a storm does to a body and to a secret. Cynical or callous, learned and unwelcome at feasts, they serve as court physician or spymaster.

The Storm Witches are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Stormlands. Stormcraft is their trade, and they treat the living with the same cold eye they turn on the sky. Cynical and callous, each is a herbalist or a physician and keeps a court alive or keeps it afraid.
civs.tagline: Hard people of the storm coast, who trust nothing unproven.

civs.name: Kioq

script.note: Signs are written in columns from top to bottom, a few to a column.

religions.name: Hanneqna
religions.desc: Hanneqna is a faith of blood, in which facing death without fear is the measure of devotion. Its sacred texts glorify willing sacrifice and teach that the god Ouqaq feeds on mortal agony and scorns weakness or doubt. Under the HuakKenVah, priestess-warriors rule from temple fortresses in the deep jungle. A Hanneqna ruler's radiance is counted in offerings, and her subjects know it.

religions.name: Biciaia
religions.desc: Biciaia is the faith of the high castes of the jungle. It teaches that souls pass through many lives and that true power lies in awaiting the gifts of destiny. Sacred marriages mark those born to command, while those of lesser birth are held to spend themselves in toil they have earned. Under the god Geevree, patience is the privilege of the well born, and the Biciane practise it with great refinement.

religions.name: Uplaialism
religions.desc: Uplaialism is a jungle faith of survival under the god Iorbrold. Its adherents believe wisdom lies in letting others spend their strength first, and they honour the lesson at feasts where the flesh of the brave and foolish is eaten. Under the HuakKenVah of the deep jungle it is a religion of warrior-priests and temple fortresses. An Uplaialist respects courage, and prefers to observe it from a distance.

civs.origin: The Kioq are the temple peoples of the central jungle. Growers, builders, traders and soldiers alike live under one holy law, delivered by warrior-priests from temple fortresses, in which martial prowess proves divine favour. Their fiercest faith is a religion of blood and of the twin-moon eclipse, where facing death without fear is the measure of devotion. Their high castes believe in rebirth and treat patience as the privilege of the well born. A third faith teaches survival by letting others spend their strength first. The priestesses keep a count of days by the moon so that no rite is missed. The Kioq regard their neighbours as offerings not yet made.

observer.label: Divided
observer.text: Putiaia, a faith of Biciaia, welcomes the visitors. Jaiokna, a faith of Hanneqna, fears them. The HuakKenVah has not chosen.

unit.name: Temple Warriors
unit.flavor: Warriors sworn to a temple, trained in its courts and sent out at its word. In the jungle they strike first and hard. In open country they are far from home.

tech_a.name: The Moon Count
tech_a.desc: The priestesses keep a count of days by the moon, cut into the temple steps and corrected every year. Every feast, fast and offering falls on a fixed day, so no rite is missed and none is held twice.

tech_b.name: The Counted Service
tech_b.desc: The moon count is turned to the people. Each household is entered on the temple rolls with the days on which it owes labour and arms, and must appear on those days with its men equipped. When the temples call a levy, the rolls already say who comes and when.

followers_desc: The Temple Guards are honoured among the Kioq. They stand watch at the pyramids and march when the temple marches. Brave or zealous, strong in arms and blunt of speech, they are knights and commanders.

The Devoted are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from Mmate. They have given their lives to the temple and count their days by the moons. Brave and zealous both, a Devoted is a jungle stalker or a holy warrior and fights in the front rank or leads it.
civs.tagline: Temple peoples of the central jungle, living under one holy law.

civs.name: Thramptith

script.medium: Stamps on wood, leather, clay or anything that takes a press
script.note: An elaborate script that few Thramptith can read. It is stamped, never drawn, by specialised writers. Their commanders are often unlettered.

religions.name: Ildliampti
religions.desc: Ildliampti is the faith of the birth-marked, the sea traders and raiders of the inner sea, who believe the goddess Chithmi marks certain children at birth for a life of service. Its adherents swear vows of poverty and give their profits to the community. Clergywomen keep the accounts in plain itciets, and the faithful count cruelty and hoarding as the gravest wrongs. The Vieunn captains who take from rich shores to feed poor harbours see themselves as her instruments.

religions.name: Ucnuioism
religions.desc: Ucnuioism is a faith of constant striving under the Mother-Goddess Erci. Its adherents, forest clans led by matriarchs, mark each step of their ascent with care and keep a strict memory of debts owed and paid. Stillness is regarded as the beginning of spiritual decay. Among the wandering forest tribes, a clan that is not moving toward something is thought to be dying.

religions.name: Veolkian
religions.desc: Veolkian is the faith of wanderers who walk the dusty paths with calm hearts and open hands. Its adherents teach by gentle deeds, wear simple robes and accept each morning as a gift from the god Zuldredrelk. They own little and ask for less. Among the forest tribes a Veolkian preacher is fed without question and listened to without being asked to speak.

civs.origin: The Thramptith are free tribes, and all of them wander: on land through the valleys, or under sail on the inner sea and the wider rivers near it. Their societies range from river communities to wild cults of nature and of beasts. Among them are striving forest clans led by matriarchs who keep a strict memory of debts, and gentle preachers who own little and ask for less. Their writing is elaborate and few of them know it. It is stamped into wood, leather, clay or anything that will take a press, by writers trained for the task, and a commander is often unable to read his own orders. They move faster than settled peoples, graze lightly and are received without hostility by strangers. They are weak in any single place and very hard to remove from the land.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: The free tribes have no teaching on the visitors.

unit.name: Freemen
unit.flavor: Free men of the clans, herders in one season and sailors in the next. They answer no summons but their own clan's, fight in loose order, and chase whatever runs.

tech_a.name: The Open Range
tech_a.desc: Herds that move with the seasons and belong to whoever drives them. A Thramptith host does not wait for wagons, because its food walks beside it.

tech_b.name: Clan Marks
tech_b.desc: Each clan cuts its own mark, and a raiding band brands or notches what it takes on the spot. No time is lost counting and quarrelling over shares on a hostile shore. The marks are read at home, and the band is gone before a levy gathers.

followers_desc: The Keepers are honoured among the Thramptith. They keep the herds and the commons of the Hollow Vales and defend both. Ambitious or patient, practical and unlettered, they serve as steward or commander.

The Guides are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Hollow Vales. They know the open range, every ford in it and how many hands a season needs. Ambitious and patient, an overseer or a forder, a Guide runs a domain well and brings a host across water without loss.
civs.tagline: Free tribes of sail and herd, poor, generous and hard to remove.

civs.name: Blouck

religions.name: Bloucca
religions.desc: Bloucca turns the loyalty of the hunting pack into a noble hierarchy. Its doctrine binds lord and vassal through ritual feasting and the symbolic eating of enemies, which is held to carry the strength of the fallen into the blood of the house. Rank is a place at the kill. The Debshas are feared by their neighbours and are perfectly courteous to one another.

civs.origin: The Blouck are a people of the southern plains who live by the law of the strong. Leadership is earned by proven strength and kept by respect and fear, shown in formal, frontal confrontation. They keep wolf-like beasts, copy their ways and run them beside their light riders. Their faith turns the loyalty of the pack into a noble hierarchy bound by ritual feasting, and rank is a place at the kill. Most are stubborn, quick to anger and ambitious, and they honour hunters above all. Neighbours fear them. Among themselves they are perfectly courteous.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Bloucca has no teaching on the visitors.

unit.name: Pack Hunters
unit.flavor: Hunters on swift Corri, with their wolf-like beasts running beside them. They do not break a line. They wait for it to break, and then nothing on the field outruns them.

tech_a.name: The Tamed Pack
tech_a.desc: The Blouck raise the wolf-like hunters of the plains from pups and run them beside their riders. The beasts follow a blood trail at a run and pull down whatever flees, and the riders have learned to hunt the same way.

tech_b.name: The Great Pack
tech_b.desc: Many packs, beast and rider together, called by one horn and hunting as the beasts do. The pack circles, cuts the weakest from the herd and does not let the wounded leave. A host that fights this way leaves fewer enemies to fight again.

followers_desc: The Pack-Runners are honoured among the Blouck. They run with the hunting packs of the plains and fight the way the pack does. Wrathful or stubborn, fierce and unschooled, they serve as knights and commanders.

The Pack-Masters are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Southern Plains. The tamed pack answers to them and to no one else. Wrathful and stubborn, a hunter or an aggressive attacker, a Pack-Master leads the charge and the pursuit after it.
civs.tagline: A plains people who live by the law of the pack.

civs.name: Preolyth

religions.name: Wicism
religions.desc: Wicism gathers its faithful around ancient trees where the spirits of ancestors are believed to dwell. There communities share modest feasts, settle old quarrels and honour those who taught forgiveness and measured living. Its groves, the moems, are known for welcome and laughter. Across the grasslands, clans that agree on nothing else will still meet under a Wicist tree.

religions.name: Jipism
religions.desc: Jipism keeps its mysteries behind welcoming doors. Its adherents join tireless work to gentle mercy and hold that any guest may carry a fragment of divine truth, so travellers are received with patience and their stories are remembered. The god Plelpa is sought in what strangers let slip. A Jipist house is an inn, a school and a shrine, in that order of appearance.

religions.name: Oltobaia
religions.desc: Oltobaia finds the divine in what has not been shaped: uncut stone, wild growth and the slow rhythm of the seasons. Its adherents contemplate these things at leisure and hold that sacred truth lies in accepting life's pleasures, not resisting them. The god Olbbul asks for no temples worth the name. A sas is usually a clearing, and its service is usually an afternoon.

civs.origin: The Preolyth are the family clans of the far south-east, the most widespread people of that quarter. Elders rule by consensus and family honour. They gather around ancient trees where the spirits of ancestors are believed to dwell, to share modest feasts and settle old quarrels, and clans that agree on nothing else will still meet there. They keep open houses that are inn, school and shrine, and some of them find the divine in whatever has not been shaped. On the whole they are a cheerful people of high morale, forgiving, hospitable and curious about strangers, and their holy places reward learning and the goodwill of other cultures.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: The clan faiths have no teaching on the visitors.

unit.name: Skirmishers
unit.flavor: Skirmishers of the islands, raised on beaches and in boats. They screen an army as a reef screens a harbour and are very hard to pin down.

tech_a.name: Tide Tables
tech_a.desc: Tables of the tides, kept by each house and added to by every generation. A Preolyth ship leaves and arrives with the water, not against it.

tech_b.name: The Far Crossing
tech_b.desc: The long voyage beyond sight of any shore, told as a story so that it can be learned by heart. A house that has made the crossing is remembered for it.

followers_desc: The Storykeepers are honoured among the Preolyth. They hold the tales of every house on the shore, the ones told aloud and the ones that are not. Patient or compassionate, good listeners and bad soldiers, they serve as chancellor or spymaster.

The Envoys are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Far Shores. An Envoy is the sworn go-between of a house, sent to live at another court, carry the word across the water and bring back what was really said. Patient and compassionate, a diplomat or a shrewd judge of people, each serves as chancellor or spymaster.
civs.tagline: Welcoming family clans of the far south-east, gathered under ancestor trees.

civs.name: Wusaun

script.medium: Ink, with a wooden pen or a bird feather
script.note: The pen gives each sign its swelling and thinning line.

religions.name: Wusaula
religions.desc: Wusaula is a network of monasteries of the open grasslands that trains quiet, patient operatives for the clans who can afford them. Its adherents follow the Master's teachings on stillness, the absence of ambition and the long wait, and may live beside a target for years. The order chooses its contracts carefully and forbids rivalry among its members. To outsiders a Wusaula house looks like any poor monastery, which is the intention.

civs.origin: The Wusaun are a quiet people of the southern plains who write in ink with a cut wooden pen or a bird feather. Their one faith looks from outside like a chain of poor grassland monasteries. Inside, it trains a few patient operatives for the clans who can afford them. Its adepts follow a teaching of stillness, the absence of ambition and the long wait, and may live beside a target for years. The order chooses its contracts with care and forbids rivalry among its own. Generally calm, content and practised in deceit, the Wusaun are rarely noticed, which is how they prefer it.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Wusaula has no stated teaching on the visitors.

unit.name: Operatives
unit.flavor: Brothers and sisters of the monasteries who are sent where an army cannot go. Few, costly and carefully trained, they fight as they do everything else, without noise.

tech_a.name: The Slow Draught
tech_a.desc: A cup prepared in the monasteries that works over days, not hours. By the time it is noticed, the one who poured it is far away and at prayer.

tech_b.name: The Long Sleep
tech_b.desc: A stillness so deep that the adept is taken for dead. Those who have returned from it are held in quiet awe, and their houses with them.

followers_desc: The Adepts are honoured among the Wusaun. They practise stillness, patience and the short blade in equal measure. Calm or content, skilled in secrets and in single combat and indifferent to wealth, they serve as spymaster or knight.

The Shades are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Southern Plains. They know the slow draught and are rarely seen before their work is done. Calm and content, a schemer or a blademaster, a Shade runs the ruler's secrets or ends a duel quickly.
civs.tagline: A quiet people of the grasslands, calm, patient and rarely noticed.

civs.name: Ogilek

script.note: The ridge braid: each consonant is a line figure cut at one slope, and its base strand links it to its neighbours, so a word forms one carved band. A second strand weaves over and under. Vowels are diamond punches above or below. This line reads "Ogilek".

religions.name: Ontlioxy
religions.desc: Ontlioxy is the faith of the people who live beneath the highlands. In carved chambers that echo with festival songs, the Ontlioxi honour the god Knoglerl by giving freely and following each enthusiasm as it comes. Their moods and devotions change often. Only one thing is fixed among them: an Ontlioxi does not lie, and expects the same of anyone admitted below.

religions.name: Blobka
religions.desc: Blobka teaches that divine power flows to those who seize an opportunity without hesitation. Its god Blobkalb is said to despise deliberation, and its adherents, the highland Boceqin, treat ambition as a holy mandate and swift, ruthless action as obedience. The faith produces leaders who join real fervour to cold calculation. In its temples the prayer of thanks is offered before the deed, not after.

religions.name: Ehlhockta
religions.desc: Ehlhockta is the faith of the Wuis, highland peoples who honour the goddess Bialkea through the body and the land together. Its rites join physical union with strict moderation, and its adherents are taught to meet wind, water and stone directly, without fear and without excess. Ehlhockta rejects both the ascetic and the glutton. Its ideal is the person who touches everything and is mastered by nothing.

religions.name: Dratana
religions.desc: Dratana teaches serenity in a world without mercy. Its adherents live in the untamed wilds of highland and grassland, watching predator and prey with patient attention, and find sacred wisdom in nature's indifference. They do not ask the god Deckerknuft for help, since none is expected. A Dratim meets hardship calmly, having studied in advance how it ends.

civs.origin: The Ogilek are the peoples of the Tulmo Plateau, and the plateau is what makes them one people. Living high and far from everyone else taught them to hold things in common: stone is worked together, stores are shared, and a guest once admitted is treated as kin. Not all of them live on the heights and their faiths differ, but most share a plain way of speaking, a dislike of lies and an open hand. They breed their Corri for slopes, fight with the sling and cut their records into stone and clay. One of their faiths has decided to fear the sky.

observer.label: Mostly undeclared
observer.text: Only Gravice, a faith of Ontlioxy, has taken a side: it fears the visitors.

unit.name: Slingers
unit.flavor: Slingers mounted on slope-bred Corri. They ride to the high ground, loose from the saddle, and are gone down a slope no pursuer will try.

tech_a.name: Slope-Bred Corri
tech_a.desc: Corri bred on the high plateau and trained from the egg on scree, ledges and steep slopes. A well-trained Corri carries a rider or a full load where a lowland animal would not set its foot, so an Ogilek host keeps its supplies with it on any ground.

tech_b.name: The Spring Pledging
tech_b.desc: Each spring every Corri chick is carried to the shrine, named before the gathered clans and pledged to the child who will ride it. The rite is also a count: the shrine keepers know how many mounts and riders each valley can send.

followers_desc: The Klomtarn are honoured among the Ogilek. They are plateau captains who lead a column and feed it too. Brave or temperate, sound in war and in stores and too plain for plots, they serve as marshal or commander.

The Glomtark are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from the Tulmo Plateau. They move hosts and slope-bred Corri over ground that stops other armies. Brave and temperate, a Glomtark is an expert of rough terrain or a logistician, and the natural marshal of a highland realm.
civs.tagline: Communal highlanders of the Tulmo Plateau, plain-spoken and generous.

civs.name: Broulqen

religions.name: Burkelo
religions.desc: Burkelo is the merchant faith of the Broulqen lands, centred on possession by the god Burqe and his spirits. Access to these rites is treated as a scarce good: who may be possessed, when, and at what offering is decided by elaborate procedure, as carefully as any contract. Its practices change over time, and its control over them does not. The Luls regard the divine as a resource that rewards good management.

religions.name: Morism
religions.desc: Morism joins settled monasteries to wandering preachers. Its influence spreads by practical charity, not doctrine: its monks hold property only in common and give regularly to those in need. In the Broulqen lands the poirs feed, heal and teach where the bureaucracy does not reach. The Morists ask no one what they believe before helping them, which has made more converts than argument ever did.

religions.name: Twulen
religions.desc: Twulen binds religion to bloodline. Its adherents, the Tiws, believe certain families carry the divine essence of the god Ibja, preserved through carefully chosen marriages. Social boundaries are rigid, and those outside the faith are expected to pay for the privilege of living beside it. The spiritual centres of the Great Irchmo govern on this basis, and their rulers present taxation as a form of grace.

religions.name: Muklutga
religions.desc: Muklutga teaches that power belongs to whoever takes it. Its god Muklu favours sudden fury, strong desire and the decision that falls like lightning, and its adherents are counselled to show one face while their real strength grows. No means of rising is forbidden. The Kilbs do not pretend otherwise, and their neighbours have learned to watch a quiet Kilb most closely.

civs.origin: The Broulqen are the people of the administered north, a country of jungle and mountain run from a capital through appointed governors who join civil rule to defence. Farmers, traders and craftsmen there live by the seal as much as the clerks do: whoever holds the office decides, and everything, the divine included, is handled by procedure. Religion matters greatly to them, and each of their faiths is an answer to one question, who may hold authority over the sacred. One says it is granted by procedure and priced like a contract. One says it runs in the blood, and presents taxation as grace. One says it belongs to whoever takes it. Where the offices do not reach, monks feed, heal and teach without asking what anyone believes. The Broulqen are for the most part careful, acquisitive and slow to change, and their holy places reward good stewardship.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: None of the four Broulqen religions has ruled on the visitors.

unit.name: Zoumbrulk
unit.flavor: Guards hired by written contract and armed with crossbows. They hold what they are paid to hold for exactly as long as the contract says.

tech_a.name: The Double Ledger
tech_a.desc: Every sum written twice, once for what is owed and once for what is held. The Broulqen clerks find the coin that single books lose.

tech_b.name: The Perpetual Debt
tech_b.desc: A loan written so that only the interest is ever paid. The principal stays in the register and passes to the debtor's heirs. Each office keeps its debtors by name, and what one harvest cannot pay is carried forward instead of forgiven.

followers_desc: The Clerks are honoured among the Broulqen. They count what comes in, count it again when it goes out and forget nothing they are owed. Greedy or stubborn, no soldiers at all, they are stewards.

The Ledger Masters are few, and they answer only a devoted ruler who holds the old knowledge and rules from Dodruvain. They keep the double ledger, where every coin is written twice and none is lost. Greedy and stubborn, avaricious or gifted administrators, they belong in the steward's chair and nowhere else.
civs.tagline: A careful people of the north, who settle land, trade and the divine by procedure.

factions.name: Onfengi
factions.text: Onfengi is the orthodox path of Dath and the faith of the old imperial houses. It preserves the wisdom of Enfu through strict adherence to classical law, some of it thousands of years old, and teaches that any change must first prove that it is not a mistake. Its realm, the Eniol Mandate, upholds order through hierarchy, surveillance and firm enforcement. It is the smallest of the four by population and holds the strongest claim to legitimacy. In script its vowels are stamped as circles and dots.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Onfengi keeps to precedent and has no teaching on the visitors.

factions.name: Panth
factions.text: Panth follows the path of Cic: rule by an enlightened few through mastery of knowledge. Its clergy are administrators and spymasters who hold that intelligence, not sentiment, keeps order. Its realm, the Eniol Technocracy, appoints governors for learning and technical skill and puts development before arms, which leaves it exposed to rougher neighbours. Panth is the one branch of Dath that looks upward. In script its vowels are stamped as diamonds, and it alone allows bright grounds in its arms.

observer.label: Welcoming
observer.text: Panth teaches that its god was born of a powerful being from beyond the sky, and that the visitors are kin returning with wisdom for those advanced enough to receive it.

factions.name: Enth
factions.text: Enth embraces the teaching of Dexa that only a single, absolute command stands between civilisation and collapse. It is the faith of generals and of those who expect to need them. Its realm, the Eniol Supremacy, takes the warrior path: lords hold their provinces by strength, keep elite retinues and regard leniency as the first sign of decay. The Quv of the Blouck serve it as levies. In script its vowels are stamped as upward triangles, in violet and gold.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Enth has no teaching on the visitors.

factions.name: Ailfaiebi
factions.text: Ailfaiebi follows the reforming vision of Pus, which holds that civilisation grows through prosperity and the affirmation of life as much as through enforcement. Its clergy favour diplomacy, trade and a justice that weighs compassion beside the letter of the law. Its realm, the Eniol Administration, governs by consensus and good relations across faiths, and prefers to persuade provinces it could command. Its elite are refined, calculating and fond of comfort. In script its vowels are stamped as geometric hearts.

observer.label: Undeclared
observer.text: Ailfaiebi has no teaching on the visitors.

news.title: Civilization gameplay, part one
news.lead: The first part of what makes each of the 21 civilizations play differently, a world without horses, a balance sweep over seven long observer games and a deep clean of the error log.
sections: Civilization gameplay
Every civilization now has the same baseline, built as one chain: two technologies, one unique unit and two tiers of followers.
The first technology is known from the start and opens the chain. The second is slow research, with a rare breakthrough from year 200.
The unique unit is raised only by rulers of the civilization's language and faith who rule from its homeland. The Xacra have two, one for each of their beasts.
On top of the baseline come special decisions, events and government mechanics, different for each civilization. More arrive with later versions.
No horses
Thekan has no horses. Riders mount the Corri, a feathered four-legged land griffon.
11 unit pictures now show Corri. Camel Riders and War Elephants show a reptilian and a shelled beast.
6 home units have pictures of their own: Ogilek Slingers, Ioddrik Ratta, Qormaic Priestess Riders, Blouck Pack Hunters, and the Xacra Scale-Beast and Shell-Beast Riders.
Mount art will be polished and extended in later versions.
Balance sweep
Knight Circles and Blouck pay more for their armies, in gold, piety and prestige.
Broulqen Bureaucracy, the Great Irchmo, the Malachite Mountain Empire, Vieunn, the Wanderers and the Meritocratic Order are strengthened.
89 noble houses of the Eniol, Broulqen, Qeomoq and Veuqrit return to the game.
Error log and bug hunt
About 60,000 errors removed from the game log.
Heirs take the government of their people on the day they inherit.
15 Earth decisions removed.

news.title: Balance and banners
news.lead: Knight Circles fight less hard, Aigl hold together slightly better, and the Broulqen bureaucracy is no longer crippled.
sections: Balance
Knight Circles are weaker in war: in long observer games they kept producing the largest realm.
Aigl under their own Stormlander rule hold together slightly better.
The Broulqen bureaucracy is less crippled. It used to die out in every long game.
Religions
Nine religions that showed a broken banner now use the default banner until they get art of their own.

news.title: Watchers and colours
news.lead: Thekan is being watched from beyond the sky, and its religions have noticed. The Observer Effect arrives, and every title on the map is recoloured by region.
sections: The Observer Effect
Pidmeddom holds that the Watchers are demons scouting an invasion. The Celestial Knights hold that they are saviours.
The two religions are hostile to each other; faiths of the same camp see each other as righteous.
Two new banner tenets with new art: Benevolent Observers and Vigilant Paranoia.
Map colours
All 3,072 title colours rebuilt. Each of the 14 regions is its own colour family, and neighbouring kingdoms contrast.
Religions rewritten
All 43 religion texts and 132 faith texts rewritten in one voice, each opening with its civilization, script and homeland.

news.title: The big map update
news.lead: Arikuri moves to Crusader Kings III 1.21 on a map more than twice as wide and tall, with rivers that follow the terrain and a world that resists easy empires.
sections: A much bigger world
The map is now 9216 x 4608 with the same 2,568 provinces.
New rivers follow the terrain down to seas and lakes: 210 river systems, 1,099 tributaries. Rivers thin out and die in the Choraman.
Jungle four times denser, other forests twice as dense: about 1.5 million trees.
14 named regions, from the Stormlands to the Far Shores.
Entropy: no easy empires
Realms past 45 counties get growing penalties, and an oversized realm can be invaded by a conqueror of another civilization.
Opening scene: Unqa of Kokaguq, a 16 year old zealot conqueror, marches on the Greenbelt and the Choraman.

news.title: Scripts, arms and a new face
news.lead: A complete visual refresh, a doubled soundtrack, and the first five writing systems in full flavour: Plith, Queekwa, Gleuncti, Pfaunkti and Aiexqelt.
sections: Writing systems
5 complete flavour systems and 17 preliminary ones, each with unique coat-of-arms templates and palettes.
Character backgrounds, tenet banners and clothing chosen by writing system.
Heraldry and sound
530+ coat-of-arms templates and 285 coloured emblems.
The soundtrack doubled in size; new main menu and loading screens.

blog.lead: The first dev diary introduced Arikuri as medieval science fiction: no elves, but many peoples with their own faces, faiths and histories.
